ozeanien-pazifik#summary: Over three millennia, Lapita seafarers and their Polynesian descendants settled the islands of the largest ocean on Earth, where distinct societies arose alongside the far older cultures of Aboriginal Australia, until European navigators, missionaries and settlers colonized the region in the 19th century.
ozeanien-pazifik#overview.0: Australia and New Guinea had been settled at least 50,000 years earlier by people whose descendants are the Aboriginal Australians and the peoples of Melanesia. The more remote islands of the Pacific, by contrast, long remained uninhabited. Around 1500 BC the Lapita culture appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago; its bearers spoke Austronesian languages, and their ancestors had come from the region of Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Within a few centuries they sailed in outrigger canoes via Vanuatu and New Caledonia as far as Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, which they reached between about 1000 and 800 BC.
ozeanien-pazifik#overview.1: In Tonga and Samoa, Polynesian culture took shape over more than a thousand years. From around the 11th century Polynesian voyagers pushed east in a rapid expansion and settled the Society Islands, the Marquesas, Hawaiʻi and Rapa Nui; around 1250 to 1300 they reached New Zealand, the last large landmass to be settled. Without instruments they navigated thousands of kilometres by the stars, ocean swells and the flight of birds. On the islands chiefdoms and kingdoms emerged, such as that of the Tuʻi Tonga; on Rapa Nui the great moai statues were carved, and in New Zealand the Māori culture developed with its fortified pā.
ozeanien-pazifik#overview.2: Aboriginal Australians lived in hundreds of language groups as hunters, gatherers and fishers who managed the land with fire and exchanged ochre, stone axes and shells along long trade routes; their world view, the Dreaming, bound them to their country. In the Torres Strait, islanders practised gardening and sea trade with New Guinea, and on the northern coast Aboriginal people met trepang fishers from Makassar from the 18th century at the latest. Europeans at first came only as visitors: Magellan crossed the Pacific in 1520/21, Abel Tasman sighted Tasmania and New Zealand in 1642, and James Cook charted many coasts and islands between 1768 and 1779.
ozeanien-pazifik#overview.3: In 1788, with the arrival of the First Fleet at Sydney, Britain founded a penal colony and took possession of Aboriginal land without a treaty. Introduced diseases, violence and the loss of land caused the Indigenous population to fall drastically. Traders, whalers and missionaries also transformed the islands: from 1797 Protestant missionaries spread Christianity from Tahiti, Kamehameha I unified Hawaiʻi with European weapons, and in New Zealand the Musket Wars between Māori tribes claimed many lives. In 1840 British officials and Māori chiefs concluded the Treaty of Waitangi, whose two versions are still understood differently today.
ozeanien-pazifik#overview.4: In the late 19th century the colonial powers divided almost all of the islands among themselves: France ruled Tahiti and New Caledonia, Germany acquired northeastern New Guinea in 1884, and in 1899 Samoa was partitioned between Germany and the United States. In New Zealand the Māori lost much of their land after the New Zealand Wars, in Australia gold discoveries drew hundreds of thousands of immigrants, and Tonga secured its independence with the constitution of 1875. In 1893 American businessmen overthrew the Hawaiian queen Liliʻuokalani, and in 1898 the United States annexed the islands. On 1 January 1901 the Australian colonies united as the Commonwealth of Australia, a federation within the British Empire in which Indigenous people, however, long had few rights.
ozeanien-pazifik#consequences.0: Polynesian languages such as Māori, Hawaiian, Samoan and Tongan are closely related and still bear witness to the common origin of the island peoples in the Lapita culture.
ozeanien-pazifik#consequences.1: The revival of traditional navigation, for example with the double-hulled canoe Hōkūleʻa, which sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments in 1976, became a symbol of Polynesian self-confidence.
ozeanien-pazifik#consequences.2: The Treaty of Waitangi is regarded as New Zealand's founding document; since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated land losses and claims by Māori tribes, leading to numerous settlements.
ozeanien-pazifik#consequences.3: The taking of Australia without a treaty shapes the debates about the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, from the recognition of native title in the Mabo decision of 1992 to the dispute over 26 January as the national day.
ozeanien-pazifik#consequences.4: Australia and New Zealand developed into immigrant societies with British-style institutions that for a long time pursued policies excluding immigrants from Asia and the Pacific.
ozeanien-pazifik#consequences.5: The annexation of Hawaiʻi made the United States a Pacific power; the Hawaiian sovereignty movement still invokes the overthrow of 1893, for which the US Congress formally apologized in 1993.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.0: Around 1500 BC the Lapita culture appears in the Bismarck Archipelago; between about 1000 and 800 BC its seafarers reach Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.1: Roughly between the 11th and 13th centuries Polynesians settle East Polynesia including Hawaiʻi and Rapa Nui, and finally New Zealand around 1250–1300.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.2: In 1521 Magellan reaches Guam after the first European crossing of the Pacific; in 1642 Abel Tasman sights Tasmania and New Zealand.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.3: From 1768 to 1779 James Cook charts the Pacific on three voyages; on 26 January 1788 the First Fleet founds the penal colony of New South Wales at Sydney Cove.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.4: By 1810 Kamehameha I has completed the unification of Hawaiʻi; in 1819 the kapu system is abolished.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.5: On 6 February 1840 the Treaty of Waitangi is signed; the New Zealand Wars follow from 1845 to 1872.
ozeanien-pazifik#keyFacts.6: In 1893 Queen Liliʻuokalani is overthrown, and in 1898 the United States annexes Hawaiʻi; on 1 January 1901 the Commonwealth of Australia is founded.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.0.paragraphs.0: In Polynesia, authority rested on descent: chiefs, called rangatira among the Māori and aliʻi in Hawaiʻi, traced their lineage back to gods and ancestors and thereby possessed mana. The larger the islands and the denser the population, the more pronounced the hierarchy. In Tonga the sacred Tuʻi Tonga stood at the top, though from the 15th century they left secular power to other lines; in Hawaiʻi several paramount chiefs fought for supremacy until Kamehameha I unified the islands. In New Zealand, by contrast, the tribes (iwi) and sub-tribes (hapū) remained independent and formed alliances only as the occasion demanded.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.0.paragraphs.1: Aboriginal Australians had neither states nor kings. Their communities were guided by older men and women who held the knowledge of land, law and ceremony; kinship systems determined who could marry whom and what obligations one had towards others. The boundaries between the territories of language groups were known, and entry into another group's country was negotiated.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.0.paragraphs.2: European colonization took different paths. Australia became a British colony in 1788 without a treaty; in the 19th century six colonies with their own parliaments emerged there and united as a federation in 1901. In New Zealand Britain invoked the Treaty of Waitangi but enforced its rule through war. Hawaiʻi and Tonga, as kingdoms, adopted constitutions on Western models, but only Tonga was able to hold its own; almost all the other island groups had become colonies or protectorates of Britain, France, Germany or the United States by 1900.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.1.paragraphs.0: Most Polynesians lived in coastal villages and hamlets, grew taro, yams, breadfruit, bananas and sweet potatoes, kept pigs, dogs and chickens and fished in lagoons and on the open sea. Land belonged to kin groups, and chiefs redistributed produce at feasts. Tapu governed what was sacred and forbidden, for example the separation of men's and women's meals in Hawaiʻi. In New Zealand, where many tropical plants did not thrive, the sweet potato, kūmara, became the most important crop, and fortified pā protected villages and food stores.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.1.paragraphs.1: Aboriginal Australians lived in small groups that moved between established campsites over the course of the year. Women gathered plants, seeds and small animals, men hunted kangaroos and emus; on coasts and rivers fishing played a major role, as the eel traps of Budj Bim in present-day Victoria attest. They managed the landscape through deliberate burning. Torres Strait Islanders, by contrast, lived as gardeners and fishers in permanent villages.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.1.paragraphs.2: Colonization fundamentally changed living conditions. Smallpox, influenza, measles and venereal diseases struck people without immunity; the population of Hawaiʻi fell to a fraction of its former size in the 19th century, and in Australia the number of Aboriginal people and their livelihoods declined sharply through disease, violence and loss of land. At the same time settler societies of convicts, free immigrants and gold seekers grew up in Australia and New Zealand, and their numbers soon exceeded those of the Indigenous peoples.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.2.paragraphs.0: The knowledge of the Pacific peoples was passed on orally: in genealogies reaching back dozens of generations, in chants, dances and stories of gods such as Tangaroa and heroes such as Māui. Navigators memorized star paths, swell patterns and landmarks; in the Marshall Islands stick charts made of palm ribs and shells served as teaching aids. Woodcarving, tattooing, bark cloth (tapa) and the feather cloaks of the Hawaiian aliʻi displayed rank and lineage.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.2.paragraphs.1: For Aboriginal Australians the Dreaming was the foundation of law and religion. Songlines described the paths of ancestral beings across the land and also served as guides over long distances. Rock art in Arnhem Land and the Kimberley, bark painting and ceremonies kept this knowledge alive.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.2.paragraphs.2: The missionaries brought Christianity, which prevailed on almost all the islands in the 19th century, often promoted by rulers such as Pōmare II on Tahiti, Kaʻahumanu in Hawaiʻi and George Tupou I in Tonga. Missionaries created written languages, translated the Bible and founded schools, so that literacy spread quickly on many islands. At the same time they suppressed dances, tattooing and older forms of belief, many of which were revived only in the 20th century.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The settlement of the Pacific rested on boatbuilding and navigation: double-hulled and outrigger canoes with sails of pandanus matting carried settlers, crops and animals across thousands of kilometres. Exchange networks linked the islands, passing on obsidian, basalt for stone adzes, mats, feathers and pottery; in the Kula ring off the eastern tip of New Guinea, shell necklaces and armbands circulated in a fixed system of exchange. In Hawaiʻi the inhabitants built large fishponds and irrigated taro fields.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.3.paragraphs.1: Aboriginal Australians, too, were linked by trade routes across the entire continent, along which ochre, stone axes, pearl shell from the north and the stimulant pituri were exchanged. From the late 18th century European and American whalers, sealers and traders arrived, buying sandalwood, sea cucumbers and coconut oil in return for ironware, cloth, alcohol and firearms.
ozeanien-pazifik#sections.3.paragraphs.2: In the 19th century Australia and New Zealand became exporters of wool, gold, wheat and later frozen meat, while Hawaiʻi and Fiji became sugar islands with workers from Asia. Tens of thousands of Melanesians were recruited for the plantations of Queensland, Fiji and Samoa, often through deception or force; this "blackbirding" is now regarded as a form of abduction. Steamships, telegraphs and, from around 1880, refrigerated ships tied the region more closely to the world economy.
suedostasien#title: Southeast Asia: From Funan to the Colonial Era
suedostasien#summary: Between India and China, trading empires, temple cities and sultanates such as Funan, Srivijaya, Angkor, Pagan, Đại Việt, Majapahit and Malacca grew up along the rivers, straits and coasts of Southeast Asia, until European companies and colonial powers had brought the whole region except Siam under their rule by 1900.
suedostasien#overview.0: Southeast Asia comprises the mainland between India and China, with the great rivers Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya, Mekong and Red River, and the island world from Sumatra to the Philippines. The monsoon winds carried ships back and forth between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea on a regular rhythm, so the region became a hub of maritime trade at an early date. From around the 1st century AD the kingdom of Funan is attested in the Mekong Delta, with its port of Óc Eo, where traders from India, China and even the Mediterranean world met. On the coast of present-day central Vietnam arose Champa, which Chinese sources mention from the late 2nd century.
suedostasien#overview.1: Through merchants, Brahmins and monks, Indian scripts, Sanskrit, Hinduism and Buddhism reached the region; local rulers adopted them by choice and blended them with their own traditions. From the late 7th century Srivijaya, based at Palembang on Sumatra, dominated the Strait of Malacca and was a centre of Buddhist learning. On Java the Shailendra and Mataram dynasties built Borobudur and Prambanan in the 8th and 9th centuries. In 802 Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire, whose capital Angkor, with Angkor Wat and the Bayon, was for centuries one of the largest cities of the preindustrial world.
suedostasien#overview.2: In what is now northern Vietnam, Ngô Quyền's victory on the Bạch Đằng River in 938 ended roughly a thousand years of Chinese rule; the later state of Đại Việt nevertheless adopted writing, Confucianism and administration from China. In Burma Anawrahta united the kingdom of Pagan from 1044, and in present-day Thailand Sukhothai emerged around 1238 and Ayutthaya in 1351. With these kingdoms Theravada Buddhism became dominant on the mainland. On Java, Majapahit rose after 1293 to become the most powerful state of the archipelago, while Islam spread along the trade routes from the late 13th century and, around 1400, the Sultanate of Malacca became the region's most important port.
suedostasien#overview.3: In 1511 the Portuguese conquered Malacca, in 1571 the Spanish made Manila the capital of their colony in the Philippines, and in 1619 the Dutch East India Company founded Batavia on Java, from where it sought to control the spice trade. For a long time, however, the Europeans remained confined to ports and islands. On the mainland strong local states held their own: the Burmese Konbaung dynasty destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, in Siam Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty at Bangkok in 1782, and in 1802 Gia Long united Vietnam under the Nguyễn dynasty.
suedostasien#overview.4: In the 19th century industrialization and imperialism shifted the balance. Britain established a trading post at Singapore in 1819, conquered Burma in three wars ending in 1885 and brought the Malay sultanates under its influence. After the Java War the Dutch forced peasants to grow export crops from 1830, and in 1887 France combined Vietnam and Cambodia into French Indochina, to which Laos was added in 1893. Only Siam, under Mongkut and Chulalongkorn, remained independent as a buffer state. In the Philippines the Katipunan rose against Spain in 1896; the independence proclaimed in 1898, however, gave way to rule by the United States.
suedostasien#consequences.0: Angkor, Borobudur, Prambanan, Pagan, Mỹ Sơn and Ayutthaya are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites and have become national symbols of the states in which they lie.
suedostasien#consequences.1: The region's religious map dates from this period: Theravada Buddhism on the mainland, a Vietnam shaped by Confucianism and Buddhism, Islam in Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei, Catholicism in the Philippines and Hinduism on Bali.
suedostasien#consequences.2: The borders of today's Southeast Asian states largely follow those of the colonial empires drawn by the British, Dutch, French, Spanish and Americans in the 19th century.
suedostasien#consequences.3: The Strait of Malacca, which had already made Srivijaya and Malacca rich, is still one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world; Singapore grew from it into one of the largest ports.
suedostasien#consequences.4: Chinese, Indian and European migrants who came with trade and the colonial economy still shape the diverse societies of Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and the Philippines today.
suedostasien#consequences.5: The experience of colonial rule, forced cultivation and exploitation fuelled the independence movements of the 20th century from Vietnam to Indonesia and shapes the region's culture of remembrance.
suedostasien#keyFacts.0: From around the 1st century AD the kingdom of Funan, with its port of Óc Eo, is attested in the Mekong Delta, linking trade routes between India and China.
suedostasien#keyFacts.1: In 682 an inscription near Palembang records the rise of Srivijaya; around 800 the Buddhist temple mountain of Borobudur is built on Java.
suedostasien#keyFacts.2: In 802 Jayavarman II founds the Khmer Empire; around 1150 Angkor Wat is built, and in 1181 Jayavarman VII takes the throne and builds Angkor Thom with the Bayon.
suedostasien#keyFacts.3: In 938 Ngô Quyền defeats a Chinese fleet on the Bạch Đằng River, ending roughly a thousand years of Chinese rule over northern Vietnam; in 1044 Anawrahta begins his reign at Pagan.
suedostasien#keyFacts.4: In 1293 Majapahit is founded on Java; around 1400 Malacca emerges, and around 1431 the Khmer kings abandon Angkor.
suedostasien#keyFacts.5: In 1511 the Portuguese conquer Malacca, in 1571 the Spanish found Manila, and in 1619 the Dutch East India Company founds Batavia.
suedostasien#keyFacts.6: In 1885 Burma becomes British, in 1887 French Indochina is created, and in 1898 the Philippines proclaim independence; Siam remains the only independent country in the region.
suedostasien#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
suedostasien#sections.0.paragraphs.0: The early states of Southeast Asia rarely had fixed borders. Historians often describe them as mandalas: around a king and his capital lay circles of princes and ports that paid tribute as long as the ruler was strong and generous, and turned to another centre when he grew weak. Power rested less on land than on people, who could be bound to the ruler, settled or carried off in war. Kingdoms such as Srivijaya, Champa or Majapahit therefore often changed their extent quickly, and their size is frequently disputed among scholars.
suedostasien#sections.0.paragraphs.1: Kings based their rule on religious ideas from India. At Angkor the Khmer rulers linked their office with Shiva, Vishnu or the Buddha and built state temples as images of the cosmic mountain Meru; Buddhist kings on the mainland saw themselves as righteous universal rulers and patrons of the monastic order. Đại Việt, by contrast, modelled itself on the Chinese imperial court, adopted civil service examinations and law codes, and formally acknowledged Chinese overlordship in order to remain independent at home. In the sultanates of the islands the ruler's dignity combined Islam with older Malay ideas of honour and loyalty.
suedostasien#sections.0.paragraphs.2: The Europeans brought a new kind of power: fortified trading posts, armed companies and later colonial administrations with fixed borders, maps and tax registers. For a long time the Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch relied on alliances with local princes. In the 19th century Britain, France and the Netherlands imposed their rule through wars, protectorate treaties and appointed officials. Siam kept its independence because its kings concluded treaties with all the powers, ceded outlying territories and modernized the state on European lines.
suedostasien#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
suedostasien#sections.1.paragraphs.0: Most people lived as rice farmers in villages along rivers and on plains, as fishers on the coasts or as swidden farmers in the uplands. The basis was wet-rice cultivation, which required a great deal of shared work on dykes, canals and fields. Nobles, priests, monks, craftsmen and dancers lived at the courts and in the temple cities; inscriptions from Angkor list thousands of servants attached to individual temples. Dependants and unfree people, often debtors or prisoners of war, were numerous in almost every kingdom, because labour was scarcer than land.
suedostasien#sections.1.paragraphs.1: In the view of many historians, women in Southeast Asia held a comparatively strong position. They worked the fields and ran markets and trade, and in many societies property was inherited through both parents. European travellers were astonished by the women traders in the ports, and there were female rulers such as the queens of Aceh in the 17th century. With the spread of Confucianism, Islam and Christianity, and under colonial law, these freedoms were restricted more tightly in many places.
suedostasien#sections.1.paragraphs.2: The great ports were highly mixed: in Malacca, Batavia, Manila or Ayutthaya, Malays, Javanese, Chinese, Indians, Arabs, Persians, Japanese and Europeans lived side by side in their own quarters. Chinese merchants and craftsmen became an important group, but also fell victim to violence, for example in massacres in Manila in 1603 and Batavia in 1740. In the 19th century hundreds of thousands of Chinese and Indians came as labourers to the tin mines and plantations of Malaya, while forced cultivation and new taxes harshly changed peasant life on Java and in Indochina.
suedostasien#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
suedostasien#sections.2.paragraphs.0: From India the elites of Southeast Asia adopted Sanskrit, scripts, epics such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and Hinduism and Buddhism, but transformed them according to their own ideas. The result was a series of unique monuments: the Buddhist temple mountain of Borobudur, the Shiva temples of Prambanan, the temples of Mỹ Sơn in Champa, Angkor Wat and the face towers of the Bayon, and the thousands of pagodas on the plain of Pagan. The story of the Ramayana lives on to this day in dance, reliefs and shadow puppetry from Java to Thailand.
suedostasien#sections.2.paragraphs.1: From the 11th century Theravada Buddhism from Sri Lanka prevailed on the mainland, and its monasteries also served as schools for village boys. Vietnam combined Mahayana Buddhism with Confucian learning and Chinese characters, and also developed its own script, Chữ Nôm. From the late 13th century Islam spread through the islands via traders, scholars and Sufis; Malay written in Arabic script became the language of commerce, religion and court literature. In the Philippines Spanish friars made Catholicism the religion of the majority.
suedostasien#sections.2.paragraphs.2: In the 19th century the printing press, newspapers and schools brought new ideas. Scholars and officials in Siam and Vietnam engaged with European science, and the Siamese court itself promoted education and translation. In the Philippines José Rizal wrote novels denouncing colonial rule and the power of the religious orders, and on Java the Dutch novel Max Havelaar by Multatuli made the suffering caused by forced cultivation widely known in 1860. At the same time European scholars began to survey the old temples and decipher their inscriptions.
suedostasien#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
suedostasien#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The monsoon winds made Southeast Asia the natural meeting point of maritime trade between the Indian Ocean and China. Ports such as Óc Eo, Palembang and Malacca thrived because ships had to wait there for the winds to change. Goods traded included Indian cotton cloth, Chinese silk and porcelain, gold, tin, fine woods, resins and above all spices: pepper from Sumatra and Java, cloves from the northern Moluccas and nutmeg from the Banda Islands, which for a long time grew nowhere else.
suedostasien#sections.3.paragraphs.1: On the mainland wealth rested on rice. Around Angkor the Khmer built huge reservoirs, canals and embankments, although scholars disagree about their role in irrigation; aerial surveys and laser scanning have shown that Angkor was a vast, sprawling urban landscape. Đại Việt protected the Red River Delta with dykes, and Burma and Siam later exported rice in large quantities. Bronze casting, shipbuilding and pottery reached a high level of skill; ceramics from Sukhothai and Vietnam were traded as far as Japan and the Middle East.
suedostasien#sections.3.paragraphs.2: The Europeans tried to control the spice trade by force: the Dutch East India Company imposed monopolies in the Moluccas and had spice trees outside its plantations destroyed. From 1565 the Manila galleon exchanged American silver for Chinese goods, linking Asia with the Americas. In the 19th century colonial rulers turned entire regions into export economies for coffee, sugar, tobacco, tin and later rubber; steamships, the Suez Canal from 1869, railways and telegraphs tied Southeast Asia closely to the world market.
byzanz#summary: The Christian, Greek-speaking Eastern Roman Empire, with its capital at Constantinople, outlived the fall of the West by almost a thousand years, held off Persians and Arabs, preserved the heritage of antiquity and shaped the Orthodox world from Greece to Russia.
byzanz#overview.0: On 11 May 330 Emperor Constantine the Great dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium, where the Bosporus links Europe and Asia. After the death of Theodosius I in 395 the Roman Empire was divided between his sons, and the East developed increasingly along its own lines. Protected by the massive Theodosian Walls and supported by the rich provinces of Asia Minor, Syria and Egypt, it survived the migration period, while the Western Roman Empire came to an end in 476. Its inhabitants continued to call themselves Romans; the term "Byzantine Empire" was coined only by early modern scholars.
byzanz#overview.1: Justinian I (527–565) set out to restore the Roman Empire within its old borders. After he had brutally crushed the Nika riots in 532, his generals, above all Belisarius and Narses, conquered the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy; a coastal strip in southern Spain was added as well. At the same time he had Roman law compiled in the work later known as the Corpus Juris Civilis and built the Hagia Sophia. But the wars, a wave of plague from 541 and pressure from the Persians overstretched the empire's resources, and in 568 the Lombards invaded Italy.
byzanz#overview.2: In the 7th century the empire fought for its survival. After a long war Emperor Heraclius defeated the Persian Sasanians in 627/628, but following the defeat at the Yarmuk in 636 the empire lost Syria, Palestine and soon Egypt to the Arabs. Constantinople withstood several Arab attacks, thanks in part to Greek fire, and Greek replaced Latin as the language of court and administration. In the 8th and 9th centuries the Iconoclast controversy over the veneration of icons divided church and society until the veneration of images was finally restored in 843.
byzanz#overview.3: Already under Michael III the missionaries Cyril and Methodius carried Christianity to the Slavs, and Bulgaria adopted the Orthodox faith. Under the Macedonian dynasty (867–1056) the empire revived: Kievan Rus became Christian, and Basil II subjugated the Bulgarian Empire by 1018. The year 1054 is regarded as the moment the Eastern and Western churches split. After the defeat by the Seljuks at Manzikert in 1071 large parts of Asia Minor were lost; the emperors of the House of Komnenos stabilized the empire and asked the West for help, which contributed to the First Crusade.
byzanz#overview.4: In 1204 the armies of the Fourth Crusade captured and sacked Constantinople and set up a Latin Empire, while Greek successor states such as Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond emerged. Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered the capital in 1261, but the restored empire remained small, weakened by civil wars and dependent on the trading cities of Venice and Genoa. From the 14th century it lost territory piece by piece to the Ottomans until Constantinople was surrounded by only a few remaining lands. With the conquest of the city by Mehmed II in 1453 the Byzantine Empire came to an end.
byzanz#consequences.0: The Roman law collected under Justinian was studied anew in Bologna from the 11th century and still forms a foundation of civil law in many countries of Europe and beyond.
byzanz#consequences.1: The Orthodox churches of Greece, the Balkans, Ukraine, Russia and the Caucasus go back to the missions and church order of Byzantium; after 1453 Russia regarded Moscow as the "Third Rome".
byzanz#consequences.2: The Cyrillic alphabet, which grew out of the mission of Cyril and Methodius, is used today for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and many other languages.
byzanz#consequences.3: Byzantine scholars preserved and commented on the works of Greek antiquity; with the manuscripts and teachers that reached Italy they contributed to the Renaissance.
